The Golden-lined sillago (Sillago analis) attains a maximum fork length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], representing the upper boundary of its size distribution across its range in northern Australian and southern New Guinean waters. This ultimate length, recorded from extensive fishery-independent surveys, positions the species among the larger members of the family Sillaginidae, though it remains notably smaller than the congeneric Sillago sihama. Concomitant with this maximum length, the species achieves an ultimate wet weight of 990 grams [Wwi = 990 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established through routine biological sampling of commercial catches. The allometric scaling between these two metrics reflects the robust, moderately deep-bodied morphology characteristic of benthic-feeding sillaginids, which invest heavily in somatic tissue to support their continuous foraging activity on infaunal invertebrates. Field observations consistently indicate that individuals approaching this asymptotic size are rare, suggesting that the population experiences substantial size-selective mortality from both predation and fishing pressure before reaching their full growth potential.

A pivotal ontogenetic milestone in Sillago analis involves the transition to reproductive competence, which is consistently reported to occur at a fork length of 22.5 cm [Lp = 22.5 cm]. This fork length at puberty marks the point at which individuals typically begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis, initiating their first spawning season within the population. The attainment of this length threshold generally corresponds to an age between one and two years under prevailing thermal regimes, though local variation in growth rates can shift this relationship. Puberty is a critical demographic parameter for this species, as it determines the age structure of the spawning stock and influences overall recruitment variability. Management strategies for the fishery often incorporate this size at maturity to establish minimum legal length limits, thereby protecting immature individuals until they have had at least one opportunity to reproduce. Comparative analyses with other sillaginids reveal that this reproductive size is consistent with the general pattern of early maturation observed in tropical members of the genus.

Laboratory-based studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C] have provided detailed insights into the species' embryonic and early larval development. Under these controlled thermal conditions, egg incubation proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days] following at a temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C] fertilization. This brief incubation period is characteristic of tropical marine teleosts that spawn small, pelagic eggs, and it minimizes the duration of vulnerability to benthic egg predators and microbial infection. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva initially weighs approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams], a value reflecting the modest egg diameter of around 0.66 millimeters. This wet weight at birth is low compared to demersal-spawning species but is typical for sillaginids that produce numerous small, planktonic propagules. The larva remains entirely lecithotrophic for the first few days, relying on endogenous yolk reserves while the mouth and digestive tract differentiate prior to the onset of first exogenous feeding.

Reproductive output in Sillago analis has been characterized through histological examination of ovaries from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. At the experimental temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], individuals are capable of producing a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 217,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 217,000 eggs per year], a value that represents the maximum observed annual fecundity for this population. This high reproductive investment is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in which females spread reproductive effort across multiple spawning events within a single season. The species is a batch spawner, releasing multiple clutches over several months to enhance the probability that at least some progeny encounter favorable planktonic conditions. The per-event fecundity and spawning frequency together determine the total annual output, which is among the highest recorded for sillaginids of comparable body size in tropical Australian estuaries. This fecundity is a direct trade-off against the relatively small size of individual eggs, each containing limited yolk reserves.

Under the same thermal regime of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], the maximum documented lifespan of Sillago analis in wild populations is 10 years [am = 10 years], a longevity that positions the species as relatively long-lived among tropical sillaginids. This lifespan was determined through otolith-based age validation studies that confirmed annual increment formation in sagittae from individuals spanning the full size range. The species' longevity is facilitated by its moderately slow growth after maturity, with asymptotic size being approached gradually over several years. The interplay between adult mortality rates and this lifespan shapes the population's resilience to exploitation, as older individuals contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the stock across multiple seasons. Senescent changes in older fish, including reduced gonad condition and slower somatic growth, have been noted in individuals exceeding eight years of age, suggesting that reproductive senescence may precede physiological death by a year or more. This extended reproductive window underscores the importance of maintaining an older age structure within the population for sustained recruitment.
